# The Burden of Proof {#sec-burden-of-proof}

In October 2014, five authors posted a preprint to arXiv under a title that reads like a legal
doctrine and is treated as one: "The Precautionary Principle (with Application to the Genetic
Modification of Organisms)" [@taleb2014precautionary]. The authors are Taleb, Read, Douady, Norman
and Bar-Yam, and their affiliations span engineering, physics, complex systems and philosophy. The
paper exists in a single version, submitted on 17 October 2014 and never revised. OpenAlex records 46 citations for it. A small number. A load-bearing argument.

This is the least cited paper in the book and the most contested. It argues for severe limits on a
technology, and it does so by turning an ethical slogan into a decision rule with conditions. Two conditions.

The chapter takes the rule apart, states what it does and does not license, and reports the
criticisms. In the book's vocabulary from Chapter 26, the rule is a **grade III claim with a grade
II argument attached**, which is the weakest combination in the scheme — and the chapter says so
before the critics do.

## Two versions of the principle

The precautionary principle is usually stated loosely: if an action might cause serious or
irreversible harm, do not take it until its safety is established.

Stated that way it is unusable, and the paper says so itself. Any action might cause harm. The
version that follows from the loose statement is "do nothing", which the authors call the paralysis
fallacy and dispose of in a section of its own.

What they propose instead is a **restricted version**, with two conditions that must hold together:

**The risk must be systemic rather than local.** First condition. A local risk has a boundary: the damage occurs
somewhere, can be isolated, can be cleaned up, and can be accounted for afterwards. A systemic risk
has no boundary; once it occurs it propagates through a network.

**The distribution must be fat-tailed.** Second condition. The extremal outcomes must be capable of ending the game
rather than merely being unlikely.

Where both hold, the paper calls the situation a **ruin problem**, and it argues that the standard
apparatus does not apply. Where either fails, ordinary cost-benefit analysis is appropriate.

| | Thin-tailed | Fat-tailed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Local exposure** | Safe: cost-benefit analysis applies | Safe, but requires strict risk management |
| **Systemic exposure** | Safe: consequences can be isolated and measured | **The domain of the precautionary principle: the burden of proof moves to the proposer** |

The table's value is that it is also a **list of where the principle does not apply**. Three of the
four cells say ordinary analysis is fine. That is what distinguishes a rule from a slogan: it can be
used to refuse, and it can be used to refuse the refusal.

## Why infinite damage cannot be averaged

The paper's hardest argument concerns permanence, and it is worth following because it is where the
rule stops being a matter of taste.

If the harm extends over all future times, the sum of the harm across time does not converge. The
integral diverges. That is not rhetoric; it is the same divergence that produced the variance
problem in Chapter 1, applied to a different integral.

Once the harm is infinite, something follows with no counterpart in ordinary risk analysis.
**any non-zero probability multiplied by an infinite harm is still infinite.** A small probability
does not tame an unbounded consequence.

The conclusion the authors draw is not "the action must never be taken". It is narrower and more
interesting: **in these problems, cost-benefit analysis is not an available tool**, because its two
sides are not in the same units. A finite benefit divided by an infinite harm is zero. The
comparison is not conservative or aggressive; it is undefined.

Alongside this sits a citation to the ruin theorems: a strategy that repeatedly accepts a small
probability of total loss will, with probability one, eventually suffer it. The point is not that
small probabilities are large. It is that **repetition converts a small per-trial probability into
a certainty, and serial decision-makers are in the repetition business.**

## The burden of proof, and why it moves

Standard practice distributes the burden: the proposer shows the benefit, the opponent shows the
harm. The paper argues that in ruin problems this allocation fails for a reason about the timing of
evidence rather than about anyone's incentives.

The sentence I would put on the cover of the paper is this one, paraphrased from the text: in ruin
problems, the claim that experience has so far provided no evidence of ruin is not a valid argument,
because **by the time the evidence arrives it will by definition be too late**. A diagnosis after
death is not a diagnosis.

From this the paper derives the rule that gives the principle its name: the burden of showing the
absence of harm falls on whoever proposes the action, not on whoever opposes it.

A second sentence matters as much: **the absence of observed harm is not evidence of the absence of
hidden risk.** That is the direct link back to Part I. Tail events are rare by construction; their
non-appearance in a sample is exactly what the distribution predicts, so non-appearance carries
almost no information.

## Where the paper says the principle does not apply

This is the part most often dropped in discussion, and dropping it converts the paper into
something it argues against.

**Vaccination is excluded.** Deliberately. The paper's criterion is systemic risk, and vaccination does not
present that structure.

**Nuclear energy is split.** Small-scale applications have harms that are comparatively limited and
better characterised, so they can be handled by cost-benefit analysis. Large-scale deployment falls
under the principle.

**Genetically modified organisms fall under it,** on the authors' argument, on systemic grounds: the authors argue that such
organisms have a propensity to spread without control, that cross-breeding prevents disentangling
modified from wild populations, and that the consequences are therefore system-wide and
irreversible. They also name a second risk source that is easy to overlook — monoculture, which
reduces the buffering capacity of the biological system independently of the modification itself.

The authors' own statement of scope is broader than the application: the aim, they write, is to
place precaution within a formal statistical and risk structure so that decision-makers can
distinguish the cases that require it from the cases where invoking it is inappropriate. The
project page says the same: applies to, but not limited to, transgenics.

**The three-way discrimination is the paper's real contribution.** Same criterion, opposite
conclusions in adjacent domains. A framework that only ever points one way is a position; one that
can refuse its own application is a tool.

## The criticisms, with their provenance

Public responses arrived within months, and they came in three forms which are worth separating
because they carry different evidential weight.

**A public critique from a scientist.** On 25 August 2014, Steven Novella, a neurologist, published
a response that is worth quoting precisely because it grants the mathematics and attacks the
application: the argument is mathematically rigorous, he wrote, but too absolute, and biologically
naive. His specific objections were that natural systems have homeostatic mechanisms so damage is
unlikely to be total, and that treating any permanent harm as infinite ignores the fact that
severity varies and that the alternatives carry risks of their own.

**A technical review and a response.** In late November 2014, Trevor Charles reviewed the paper,
questioning among other things the absence of a definition of "genetically modified", the assertion
of uncontrolled spread without citation, and the conflation of monoculture with modification. The
following day the five authors published a point-by-point response. One sentence from it identifies
the real disagreement: they state that they did not perform a statistical analysis but a rigorous
analysis of risk as derived from probability theory. **That is the crux. Two disciplines, two questions. The reviewers asked for
data; the authors answered that their subject was the structure of the argument.**

**The authors' own assessment**, which must be labelled as such: on their project page they state
that they had received no credible or relevant technical comment. This is a party's account of its
own reception, not a finding, and it is recorded here as a position rather than as fact.

| When | Who | Substance | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2014-08-25 | Novella, public blog | Mathematical rigour granted; absolute and biologically naive; treats all permanent harm as infinite | Public criticism |
| 2014-11-27 | Charles, technical review | Undefined terms; uncited spread claim; monoculture conflation | Peer-style review |
| 2014-11-28 | The five authors | Point-by-point reply; characterises the work as probability-theoretic rather than statistical | Author response |
| Undated | Authors' project page | States no credible technical comment received | **Party's own account** |

One common attribution should be avoided. The best-known attacks on precaution as a policy
principle — on its costs, and on its coherence — are general critiques of the idea. I found no
evidence that they were aimed at this paper, and they are not counted here as criticisms of it.
**Attaching a general objection to a specific paper is the commonest distortion in this literature.**

## Grading the rule

Using the vocabulary of Chapter 26.

**The criterion is a construction.** A filter, not a finding. No evidence attaches to it. Nothing about the intersection of systemic exposure and fat
tails is an empirical finding. It is a proposed filter, and its authors present it as one.

**The infinite-harm argument is a grade II claim.** It survives changes of distribution family,
because it rests on divergence rather than on a parameter, and it does not survive a change of the
object: for a reversible harm, the integral converges and the argument evaporates.

**The procedural rule is grade III.** The weakest grade. "In irreversible situations the burden falls on the proposer"
refers to no measurable quantity. It cannot be supported by data in the way lower grades can, which
is exactly the weakness the last round of critique identified.

The combination is uncomfortable and worth naming. **A grade III prescription resting on a grade II
argument is the standard shape of a policy paper, and it is the shape most vulnerable to the
objection that the prescription is doing more work than the argument supports.**

## Claim and tool

The claim: that precaution, properly restricted, identifies a class of decisions where the standard
apparatus is structurally inapplicable rather than merely imprecise.

The tool: the two-condition filter, the ruin framing, the burden-of-proof shift, and — most
durably — the discrimination list, which demonstrates that the filter can be applied against the
interests of whoever is invoking it.

## Boundary conditions

The rule applies only where systemic exposure and fat tails coincide, and both conditions must be
argued rather than asserted. Where exposure is local, the rule is silent and cost-benefit analysis
resumes.

It fails where the harm is reversible, because the divergence argument requires permanence.

It fails as a general policy filter, because most policy problems are local in the relevant sense.
**The paper's own three-way discrimination is the proof that it cannot be used as a blanket
doctrine.**

And it inherits the estimation problem of Part I: deciding whether a risk is systemic is a
judgement about mechanisms and networks, often made with less information than the judgement
deserves.

## The cost of shifting the burden

The burden-of-proof rule is a procedural instruction, and like every procedural instruction it has
costs. Stating them is part of using the rule honestly.

**It slows beneficial deployment.** That is the price. A proposer who must demonstrate the absence of harm
before proceeding will proceed less often, and some of what does not proceed would have been
beneficial. The framework does not measure this cost, and its critics are right that the cost is real.

**It rewards the status quo asymmetrically.** Usually. The rule applies to proposals for change, and the
existing arrangement is not required to demonstrate its own safety. Where the status quo carries the
same systemic exposure as the proposal, the asymmetry is arbitrary and the rule should be applied
against the incumbent instead. **The criterion's indifference to whether the action is doing or
refraining is what makes that application possible, and it is also what makes it rare.**

**It can be captured.** Any burden can. A rule that requires demonstration of safety is a rule that can be used to
delay a competitor. This is a general property of procedural burdens rather than a defect of this
one, and the defence is the same as for every device in this book: the record of who invoked it and
for what.

**The cost that the rule is buying protection against.** Where the exposure is genuinely systemic and
irreversible, the cost of a delayed benefit is paid in the currency of foregone improvement, and the
cost of a premature deployment is paid in the currency of an absorbing state. **The rule's claim is
that the second currency is different in kind, not that it is larger.**

**What would weaken the rule substantially.** Evidence that the screening cases are rare — that most
technologies and policies are local and reversible, so that the rule's scope is narrow and its costs
are borne by a few decisions rather than many. **I think that is probably true, and it is an argument
for the rule being applied sparingly rather than an argument against its existence.**

## The rule as a test of the proposer

The burden-of-proof rule is usually read as a constraint on proposals. Read the other way, it is a
diagnostic that a proposer can apply to their own case, and the diagnostic is more useful than the
constraint.

**Three questions a proposer can ask.**

**What is the failure mode if I am wrong, and is it bounded?** First question. Where the failure is bounded, the
burden allocation is irrelevant and the ordinary case for the proposal stands.

**Can I demonstrate the absence of the harm, or only its low probability?** Second question. The rule
asks for the former. **A proposer who can only offer the latter is asking to be permitted a risk rather
than demonstrating its absence, which is a different request and should be made explicitly.**

**Would I accept the same argument from the opposite side?** Third question. The symmetry test. Where the
argument works only in one direction, it is advocacy.

**What the diagnostic changes.** A proposer who runs it either arrives at a bounded failure mode — in
which case the proposal proceeds on ordinary grounds — or discovers that the failure mode is
unbounded, at which point the useful move is to change the proposal rather than to argue about the
rule.

**Two examples of the second outcome.**

**A deployment with an exit the organisation cannot secure.** Unbounded in time. The failure mode
is unbounded in time, not in damage. The remedy is contractual: secure the exit before deploying.

**A visible commitment.** Self-fulfilling. The failure mode is social and
irreversible. The remedy is the pre-committed review, which converts a later judgement into a decision
made now.

**Why this framing is worth the section.** Because the burden rule is otherwise a demand made of other
people, and a demand made of other people is resisted. **A test a proposer runs on their own case is
adopted; a rule imposed on the proposer is litigated.**

## The three ways the rule is evaded

Procedural rules fail through evasion more often than through disagreement, and the three evasions of the
burden rule are worth naming because each has a recognisable form.

**Evasion one. Redefine the exposure as local.** The claim that consequences are confined to identifiable
parties, made without examining the network. **The tell is that the confinement is asserted rather than
demonstrated, and the demonstration is usually a diagram nobody has drawn.**

**Evasion two. Move the demonstration to a later stage.** Commit now, demonstrate safety later, with the
promise of an exit if the demonstration fails. **The tell is that the exit requires an agreement, and the
agreement has not been obtained.**

**Evasion three. Treat the absence of observed harm as the demonstration.** This is the evasion the rule
exists to block, and it is the most common. **The tell is a sample whose size is described but whose
sensitivity is not, since the argument depends on how much harm the sample would have detected.**

**How to test for each.** One question apiece.

**Evasion one.** Name the propagation path or state that it does not exist. **An actor who cannot name either
has asserted locality rather than established it.**

**Evasion two.** Exit needs consent. Name who must agree and whether they have. **If the counterparty's agreement is
required and has not been sought, the exit is not an exit.**

**Evasion three.** Say what magnitude of harm the sample would have detected with reasonable probability. **A
sample that could not have detected the harm carries no information, and computing the detectable magnitude
takes a power calculation rather than a new dataset.**

**Why the evasions are worth listing.** Because the rule is otherwise a principle that everyone agrees with
and nobody applies, and the evasions are what applying it looks like from the inside. **Three questions turn a
principle into a check, which is what the rule needs to be in a meeting.**

## Precaution and the regulator's problem

The rule's costs fall on proposers. Regulators face the mirror image, and their situation is worth stating
because it explains why the rule is applied inconsistently.

**The regulator's asymmetry.** Structural, not moral. Incentives, again. Approving something harmful is a visible failure with an
identifiable decision behind it. Refusing something beneficial is an invisible failure with no decision to
point at. **The incentive therefore favours refusal, and the cost is borne by whoever would have benefited.**

**Three consequences.**

**Approval standards drift upward.** Each approved risk that materialises adds a requirement, and no
countervailing pressure removes requirements. The drift is not corruption; it is the accumulation of
visible failures.

**Beneficial innovations are delayed by the length of the review rather than by its outcome.** The delay
costs lives in the aggregate and appears in no record.

**The burden shifts to small proposers.** Compliance costs are fixed, so they fall hardest on those with the
least capacity. **A rule intended to protect the public can function as a barrier to entry, and the effect
is invisible in the rule's text.**

**What the framework contributes.** Not a correction of the incentive, which is structural. What it
contributes is a vocabulary for stating the trade: **which exposure is systemic, which is local, and what
scale is available between refusal and full deployment.** The scale question is the regulator's real
instrument, because a pilot with monitoring is neither approval nor refusal.

**What it cannot contribute.** The exchange rate. The exchange rate between a delayed benefit and an avoided harm. **That is a
political question, and the framework's value is to make it explicit rather than to settle it.**

## The rule and the cost of being wrong twice

The burden rule shifts who must demonstrate safety. Its weakest point is the case where the harm is avoided and
the benefit is lost, and the loss is invisible.

**The asymmetry restated. Two errors.**

**Approving a harmful exposure.** Visible, attributable, and followed by a tightening of standards.

**Refusing a beneficial one.** Invisible, unattributable, and followed by nothing.

**Why the second is larger in aggregate.** Because approvals are individually scrutinised and refusals are not.
**Each decision is small and the accumulation is not, and no actor's record reflects the aggregate.**

**Three mechanisms that amplify the invisibility.**

**No counterfactual.** The benefit not realised leaves no trace in any dataset.

**Diffuse beneficiaries.** The losers from a refusal are many and unorganised; the potential losers from an
approval are identifiable and mobilised.

**Selection in the record.** Approved risks that materialise generate evidence; refused benefits do not.
**The historical record is therefore biased toward the case for caution, and the bias is structural.**

**What the framework offers against this.** The negative list, which is the only part of the apparatus that names
the cases where the answer is to proceed. **A framework whose output is always caution is not a framework, and
the list is what distinguishes one from a disposition.**

**What it cannot offer.** An estimate of the aggregate cost of refusals. **That quantity would require a
counterfactual record that no institution keeps, and its absence is itself the reason the asymmetry
persists.**

**The practical implication.** A practitioner applying the rule should ask, for each case, what the cost of a
wrong refusal would be, and write it down. **Writing it down does not make the cost visible to the institution,
but it makes it visible to the decision.**

## The rule and the record it leaves

The burden rule is a procedural instrument, and procedures are judged by the record they generate. This
section states what a good record contains, because a rule with no record is a rule that cannot be audited.

**Three items per decision.**

**One. Which condition was examined, and by whom.** Systemic exposure or not, fat tailed or not. **The
examiner's identity matters: a condition examined by the proposer is examined differently from one examined
independently.**

**Two. What evidence was offered for the examination.** A diagram of the propagation path, a measurement of
the tail, or an assertion. **The three are distinguishable in a record and indistinguishable in a summary.**

**Three. What the proposer was required to demonstrate, and what was accepted.** Which is where the burden
rule is either applied or evaded. **The evasions of the earlier section leave specific traces: a locality
asserted, an exit promised without consent, a sample whose sensitivity was not stated.**

**What the record prevents. Two failures.**

**The rule being cited without being applied.** A minute that says the principle was considered is not a
record of an examination.

**The conditions being re-litigated at each stage.** A record of what was examined, and when, is what stops
the same argument from being run again at the review.

**What the record cannot do.** Make the examination correct. **It makes the examination visible, which is the
most a procedural instrument can achieve and the reason the rule is worth having.**

**Why the record is the chapter's practical output.** Because the rule is a principle that everyone agrees
with, and its application is the three items above. **A principle without a record is a disposition; a
principle with one is a procedure.**

## The rule and three kinds of demonstration

The burden shifts to the proposer. What counts as a demonstration differs by case, and three kinds appear.

**A demonstration that the exposure is local.** A propagation path that stops, or an argument that it cannot
start. **Which answers the first condition and is the commonest form, and the one most often asserted rather than
shown.**

**A demonstration that the harm is reversible.** A recovery time, a clean-up cost, a restorable state. **Which
answers the third condition and is the form most often available and least often offered.**

**A demonstration that the scale is bounded.** A pilot, a cap, a staged commitment. **Which answers neither
condition and satisfies the rule anyway, because a bounded exposure is not a ruin problem.**

**What the three have in common. One property.** Each is structural and none requires a probability. **Which is
what makes the rule applicable where the quantities may not exist, and it is the reason the framework belongs in
the same part as the ledger.**

**Which is strongest. The third.** Because it does not depend on any empirical claim about propagation or
reversibility and can be adopted unilaterally by the proposer. **Which is why the book's practical advice is often
a scale.**

**Which is weakest. The first.** Because locality is easy to assert and hard to establish, and the assertion is
the framework's own evasion. **The demonstration requires a path or a reason, not a boundary drawn on a
diagram.**

**What a proposer should offer. The third, plus whichever of the first two is available.** Which is a pilot with a
bounded loss and a stated recovery time, and which satisfies the burden in a paragraph. **Three demonstrations,
and the one that requires no empirical claim is the one to lead with.**

Three demonstrations. Locality. Reversibility. Scale. Offer the third. Then the others.

## A note on what this chapter could not check

The derivation in the paper's appendix was not available to me, and none of its formulas are
reproduced here. The arguments above are taken from the paper's text as available, from the authors'
separate exposition, and from the published responses; where the book paraphrases rather than
quotes, it says so.

The 2018 citations to a "precautionary principle" paper that appear in some later work are, on the
evidence available, secondary citations of this 2014 preprint rather than references to a separate
2018 text. This book therefore cites the preprint, and does not treat a 2018 paper as existing.

And the content of the two responses is described at the level of their published summaries and the
authors' reply. I read neither in full.
